lectures.name: Anatomy of the Anterior Abdominal Wall

blocks.html:
Layers of the anterior abdominal wall (superficial → deep)

skin → Camper’s fascia (fat) → Scarpa’s fascia (membranous) → deep fascia → aponeuroses of the muscle layers → external oblique (investing fascia) → internal oblique (investing fascia) → transverse abdominis (investing fascia) → transversalis fascia → extraperitoneal fat → parietal peritoneum

Arcuate line

Demarcates where the aponeurotic components of the anterior and posterior rectus sheath change.

  • Superior to it: external oblique + internal oblique pass anteriorly; internal oblique + transverse abdominis pass posteriorly
  • Inferior to it: external oblique + internal oblique + transverse abdominis all pass anteriorly; only transversalis fascia passes posteriorly
Planes and regions
  • Transpyloric plane: landmark for gallbladder, neck of pancreas, SMA, hepatic portal vein, root of transverse mesocolon, duodenojejunal junction, renal hila
  • The nine regions are bounded by the midclavicular planes (vertical) and the subcostal and transtubercular planes (horizontal)

blocks.html:
Inguinal region
  • Inguinal canal: the testes and spermatic cord (males) and round ligament (females) descend through it during embryonic development
  • Hesselbach’s triangle: inferior epigastric artery, rectus abdominis, inguinal ligament; site of direct hernias
  • Femoral triangle: inguinal ligament, adductor longus muscle, sartorius muscle
Spermatic cord
  • Fascial layers (derived from the abdominal wall): transversalis fascia → internal spermatic fascia; internal oblique → cremaster muscle and fascia; external oblique → external spermatic fascia
  • Contents: ductus deferens, testicular artery, testicular vein, genital branch of genitofemoral nerve
Peritoneum
  • Parietal peritoneum: outer membrane lining the deep surface of the abdominal walls and the inferior surface of the diaphragm
  • Peritoneal cavity: a narrow, potential space between the opposing layers of peritoneum
  • Visceral peritoneum: inner membrane that directly covers the abdominal organs

blocks.html:
Peritoneal folds (anterior abdominal wall)
  • Median umbilical fold – obliterated urachus
  • Medial umbilical fold – obliterated umbilical artery
  • Lateral umbilical fold – inferior epigastric vessels
Recesses and mesenteries
  • Morison’s pouch (hepatorenal recess): the deepest part of the peritoneal cavity when supine – accumulates fluid
  • Dorsal mesentery: attaches caudal foregut, midgut and hindgut to the dorsal body wall; pulled to the left; envelops spleen → lesser sac (omental bursa); greater omentum (gastrophrenic, gastrosplenic, gastrocolic ligaments)
  • Ventral mesentery: attaches caudal foregut to the ventral body wall; pulled to the right; envelops liver (falciform ligament) → greater sac; lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal, hepatogastric ligaments)
Pectinate line

Divides the anal canal at the hindgut–proctodaeum junction.

Blood supply and venous systems
  • Watershed zones: receive dual supply from the most distal branches of two large arteries – vulnerable to ischemia
    • Splenic flexure: terminal branches of the SMA and IMA
    • Sigmoid colon: terminal branches of the inferior mesenteric, pudendal and iliac circulations
  • Azygos system: anastomosis between SVC and IVC; azygos vein (R), hemiazygos vein (L)
  • IVC system: drains the lower half of the body into the RA; R/L common iliac veins, R/L gonadal/suprarenal veins
  • Portal system: portal vein drains spleen, intestine and colon into the liver; hepatic veins drain into the IVC

Lymphatics and GALT
  • Lymphatic drainage from GI viscera: see chain below; enters the systemic circulation at the left venous angle
  • Peyer’s patches / GALT: aggregates of lymphoid tissue throughout the lamina propria and submucosa of the digestive tract
    • Microfold (M) cells sample antigen in the lumen and present it to antigen-presenting cells
    • B cells stimulated in germinal centres become IgA-secreting plasma cells in the lamina propria

blocks.html:
Nerve supply of the GI tract

Controls secretion, motility, pain sensation, intestinal reflexes and vascular tone.

  • Extrinsic = autonomic nervous system
    • Sympathetic: paravertebral and prevertebral ganglia (celiac, mesenteric) → splanchnic nerves; preganglionic NT = ACh; postganglionic NT = norepinephrine – inhibitory (↓ gastric emptying, vasoconstriction)
    • Parasympathetic: vagus and pelvic nerves; excitatory = ACh (enhances GI function); inhibitory = NO and VIP (smooth muscle relaxation, ↓ GI function)
  • Intrinsic = enteric nervous system (ENS): ganglionic plexuses entirely within the gut wall, esophagus to anus; NT = neuropeptides
    • Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: coordinates motility along the full length of the gut
    • Submucosal (Meissner) plexus: regulates secretion, blood flow and absorption
Abdominal pain
  • Parietal pain = localized, sharp – shares somatic innervation with the abdominal wall
  • Visceral pain = diffuse, cramping – no somatic nerve supply

blocks.html:
Layers of the gut wall

Mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae) → submucosa (with Meissner plexus) → muscularis externa (inner circular, Auerbach plexus, outer longitudinal) → serosa.

blocks.alt: Gut wall layers – note the two nerve plexuses: submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) between the muscle layers.
blocks.cap: Gut wall layers – note the two nerve plexuses: submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) between the muscle layers.

Biliary tree
  • Drainage: see chain below – empties into the descending (2nd) part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla
  • Portal triad = common hepatic duct + hepatic portal vein + proper hepatic artery; runs in the hepatoduodenal ligament
  • Triangle of Calot: cystic duct, liver, common hepatic duct; landmark for the cystic artery
Embryological remnants of the liver
  • Ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum
  • Umbilical vein → round ligament of the liver (ligamentum teres)

lectures.title: Anatomy of the Abdominal Wall & GI Tract
lectures.framing: A tour of the abdomen from the outside in: wall layers and regions, the peritoneum and its folds, then the vessels, lymphatics and nerves of the gut. The organising idea is embryological origin – it predicts blood supply, drainage and innervation (the pectinate line is the clearest example).
lectures.keypoints: Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus. Hesselbach’s triangle = direct hernias. Retroperitoneal organs: SAD PUCKER. The pectinate line splits the anal canal: above = autonomic, portal, columnar; below = somatic, caval, squamous. Portal hypertension shows at the esophagus (varices), umbilicus (caput medusae) and rectum. Watershed zones: splenic flexure and sigmoid.

lectures.name: PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs

blocks.html:
Mechanisms of mucosal defence
  • Sphincters: keep acid contained in the stomach, protecting the esophagus and intestines
  • Bicarbonate: neutralizes the acid
  • Blood flow: washes away some of the acid that gets into the gastric mucosa
  • Mucus: protective layer over the epithelial cells; protects the gastric mucosa from abrasion
Options for ulcer / reflux treatment
  • ↓ gastric secretion by inhibiting histamine receptors and/or the proton pump in parietal cells
  • ↑ mucosal defences with prostaglandin analogues (stimulate mucus and bicarbonate)
  • ↑ tone and esophageal motility (prokinetics)
  • Treat H. pylori infection with ABX
  • Treat symptoms by neutralizing acid (antacids) and/or drugs that cover and soothe ulcers

lectures.name: Diarrhea & Malabsorption

blocks.html:
Definitions
  • Normal bowel movements: 3/day to 1 every 3 days; normal stools are isosmotic
  • Diarrhea: abnormal frequency and liquidity of fecal evacuations – the water balance of the GI tract is disturbed
    • > 3 BMs/day, stool weight > 200 g/day
    • Acute < 4 weeks – usually infectious; chronic > 4 weeks – usually non-infectious

blocks.alt: First split by duration, then by blood: acute bloody = dysentery; chronic bloody = IBD; chronic non-bloody = IBD, celiac, microscopic colitis.
blocks.cap: First split by duration, then by blood: acute bloody = dysentery; chronic bloody = IBD; chronic non-bloody = IBD, celiac, microscopic colitis.

rows: Osmotic: too much water drawn into bowels
Ingestion (laxatives), maldigestion (pancreatic insufficiency, disaccharidase deficiency), malabsorption (celiac disease), Toddler’s diarrhea (juice)
Neuroendocrine tumours (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), cholera, chemical stimulants, hormones (VIP)

blocks.html:
Stool osmotic gap

Osmotic gap = 290 – 2([Na+] + [K+]) (stool electrolytes) – measures the difference in solute types between serum and feces.

  • > 50 mOsm/L → osmotic diarrhea
  • < 50 mOsm/L → secretory diarrhea
  • Most diarrheas are a mixture of secretory and osmotic components

Diarrhea workup
  • Hx: nature of diarrhea (acute/chronic, bloody/non-bloody, frequency, steatorrhea), fecal urgency, incontinence, abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, energy level; risk factors (medications/ABX, foreign travel, sick contacts, dietary Hx/water source, ethnicity); extraintestinal manifestations of IBD (mouth ulcers, perianal disease, skin rash, eye symptoms, arthritis)
  • PEx: vital signs (fever, dehydration), weight, nutritional status, abdominal exam
  • Ix: CBC, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, ESR, CRP, lipid profile, glucose, pancreatic enzymes, albumin, blood cultures, AXR; microbiology (stool C&S, stool O&P, C. difficile toxin); α-1 antitrypsin, TTG, sigmoidoscopy
  • Consider admission: severe systemic signs, cannot maintain hydration orally, infants, elderly, immunocompromised

Drugs associated with diarrhea

Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, alcohol, ABX, antidiabetics, cholinergic agonists, dopamine antagonists, H2-receptor antagonists, immunosuppressants, levothyroxine, laxatives, orlistat (lipase inhibitor), potassium supplements, prostaglandins, SSRIs, sulfasalazine.

Non-inflammatory infectious diarrhea

Enterotoxin-mediated change in fluid/electrolyte absorption/secretion; small intestine.

  • Vibrio cholerae serotypes O1 and O139 (gram-negative rod): rice-water diarrhea (mechanism below)
    • Tx: oral/IV rehydration, ABX (doxycycline, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin); prevention (sanitation, Dukoral vaccine)
  • Food poisoning: E. coli O157:H7 (verotoxin), S. aureus, Bacillus cereus
  • Watery diarrhea: norovirus, rotavirus, Giardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora belli

blocks.html:
Inflammatory infectious diarrhea

Cytotoxin-mediated destruction/invasion of mucosal cells; large intestine. Abdominal cramping, fever, bloody stools.

  • Bacterial bloody diarrhea (CC-E-YSS): Clostridium difficile, Campylobacter jejuni (poultry), E. coli O157:H7, Yersinia enterocolitica, Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi (typhoid fever), Shigella dysenteriae; Vibrio vulnificus
  • Parasitic bloody diarrhea: Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia

blocks.title: Bloody infectious diarrhea
blocks.html: NEVER give antidiarrheal agents – they prolong exposure to the organism → toxic megacolon.

Malabsorption

Inadequate absorption of nutrients from the GI tract – the small bowel is especially important.

blocks.html:
Pediatric diarrhea
  • Excessive daily stool: liquid volume > 10 mL stool/kg/day; acute < 2 weeks, chronic > 2 weeks
  • Red flags: chronicity; blood/mucus/undigested food; minimal or no weight gain / weight loss; nighttime stooling; output ≫ intake; no response to stopping intake
  • Celiac disease: abdominal pain/distension, loose non-bloody stools, iron deficiency, poor growth – test total IgA + TTG IgA
  • Milk protein intolerance: mucus in stool ± blood, regurgitation, otherwise healthy – dairy-free diet, hydrolyzed protein formula
  • Assess hydration in any acute diarrheal illness – oral rehydration is the most important Tx
  • Check a stool culture before starting ABX

lectures.title: Diarrhea & Malabsorption
lectures.framing: Diarrhea is a disturbance of the gut’s water balance. The approach sorts it by duration (acute = infectious, chronic = non-infectious), then blood, then mechanism (osmotic, secretory, inflammatory, motility) – the stool osmotic gap separates the first two.
lectures.keypoints: Diarrhea = > 3 BMs/day or > 200 g/day; acute < 4 weeks. Osmotic gap > 50 = osmotic, < 50 = secretory. Small bowel = large volume, infrequent; large bowel = small volume, urgent. Cholera toxin ↑ cAMP → Cl– secretion. Bloody infectious diarrhea (CC-E-YSS): never give antidiarrheals. In children, oral rehydration is the key treatment.

lectures.name: Constipation

blocks.html:
Rome IV criteria – functional constipation

Must include ≥ 2 of the following:

  1. Straining in > 25% of defecations
  2. Lumpy or hard stools (Bristol 1 or 2) in > 25% of defecations
  3. Sensation of incomplete evacuation in > 25% of defecations
  4. Sensation of anorectal obstruction/blockage in > 25% of defecations
  5. Manual maneuvers to facilitate > 25% of defecations (digital evacuation, support of the pelvic floor)
  6. < 3 spontaneous BMs per week

Plus:

  • Loose stools rarely present without laxatives
  • Insufficient criteria for IBS
  • Criteria fulfilled for the last 3 months with symptom onset ≥ 6 months before Dx

blocks.alt: Bristol stool chart: types 1–2 = constipation (the Rome IV criterion), 3–4 = normal, 6–7 = diarrhea.
blocks.cap: Bristol stool chart: types 1–2 = constipation (the Rome IV criterion), 3–4 = normal, 6–7 = diarrhea.

Metabolic: hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, diabetes
Structural: colorectal cancer, benign strictures, pseudo-obstruction
Neurologic/myopathies: Parkinson’s disease, MS, spinal cord injury, autonomic neuropathy, Hirschsprung’s, immobility, botulism, hollow visceral myopathy, cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy

Systemic: trisomy 21, cystic fibrosis, connective tissue disorders, celiac disease, cow’s milk allergy

Anismus: the paradoxical contraction of the anal sphincter rather than relaxing during attempted defecation
Dyssynergia: any disturbance of muscular coordination, resulting in uncoordinated and abrupt movements
Rectocele: a bulging of the front wall of the rectum into the back wall of the vagina

blocks.html:
Constipation workup
  • Hx: symptoms, dietary Hx (fibre/water), adequate time for toileting, willingness to use public bathrooms, PMHx (look for 2° causes), medications, allergies, social Hx (ADLs, IADLs, abuse)
  • PEx: DRE – inspect for anal fissures/hemorrhoids/soiling, anal tone at rest and with squeeze, palpate for rectal mass, exclude fecal impaction
  • Ix: CBC, calcium, TSH; colonoscopy for red flags
    • Colon transit study: 24 radio-opaque Sitz markers swallowed on day 1; AXR on day 5
    • Anorectal manometry + balloon expulsion: pressure catheter and balloon in the rectum measure rectal sensation, anal pressure, anorectal inhibitory reflex and ability to expel the balloon
    • Defecating proctogram: barium instilled into the rectum, then defecation on a commode under x-ray – shows anatomic abnormalities
Treatment
  • Patient education; diet/lifestyle – adequate fluid, 20–30 g/day fibre, physical activity
  • Osmotic laxatives: PEG 3350 17 g in 8 oz water; lactulose 15–30 cc; magnesium-based
  • Stimulant laxatives: senna 1 tab; bisacodyl 5 mg
  • Stool softeners: docusate 100 mg b.i.d.; mineral oil 15 mL – NOT recommended (lack of efficacy)
  • Enemas: sodium phosphate, tap water, soap suds
  • Secretagogues: linaclotide (145 mcg constipation, 290 mcg IBS-C); prucalopride
  • Surgery: subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis; rectocele repair
  • Biofeedback: relaxation/coordination retraining of the pelvic floor
  • PEG 3350 has no electrolytes and is tasteless; PegLyte is the bowel prep before colonoscopy

blocks.title: Myths and Choosing Wisely
blocks.html:
• Long-term laxative use will NOT cause dependency or a “lazy colon”
  • Do NOT colonoscope for constipation under age 50 without a family history of colon cancer or alarm features

blocks.html:
Colorectal cancer – epidemiology
  • New cancer cases: 3rd (M, F); cancer deaths: 2nd (M), 3rd (F)
  • Commonest cause of cancer death in non-smokers
  • Sporadic 90–95%; hereditary 5–10%
  • Almost all CRCs arise from polyps
Polyps
  • Conventional adenoma (tubular, tubulovillous, villous): head and stalk easily removed at biopsy
  • Sessile serrated adenoma: common on the R side, flat/fusiform, cancers associated with microsatellite instability, easily missed
Colorectal cancer workup
  • Etiology: environmental (diet, physical activity), IBD (Crohn disease, UC)
  • Non-GI symptoms = R-sided colon cancers: anemia, weight loss
  • GI symptoms = L-sided colon cancers: rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, diarrhea/constipation, mass on DRE
  • Ix: DRE, double-contrast barium enema (“apple core” lesions), colonoscopy/sigmoidoscopy + biopsy; staging: CXR, CT chest/abdomen
  • Spread: direct extension (bladder, vagina, skin, other bowel), metastases (lymph nodes, hematogenous), transperitoneal
Pathological staging

Acute liver failure

Coagulopathy (INR ≥ 1.5) + neurologic dysfunction with any degree of hepatic encephalopathy, no prior liver disease, course ≤ 26 weeks.

  • Causes: acetaminophen, DILI, HBV, HAV, autoimmunity, ischemia, Wilson’s disease, Budd-Chiari, pregnancy
  • Ix: serum chemistries, hepatic panel, arterial blood, toxicology, hematology, viral hepatitis serologies, autoimmune markers, urine, serum ceruloplasmin, blood cultures, ECG, imaging
  • Tx: routine monitoring, glucose infusions, stress ulcer prophylaxis, restrict clotting factors unless actively bleeding, N-acetylcysteine, avoid sedatives and hepatotoxic/nephrotoxic drugs
  • Hepatic encephalopathy: transfer to critical care at the first mental change; quiet surroundings, elevate head of bed, intubate, ventilate, sedate; empirical ABX; normalize Na, Mg, PO4, K

blocks.html:
Chronic hepatitis (> 6 months) – causes
  • Viral: HBV, HCV, HDV
  • Autoimmune: autoimmune hepatitis, PBC, PSC, IgG4 cholangiopathy
  • Chronic biliary disease: recurrent bacterial cholangitis, bile duct stenosis
  • Cardiovascular: Budd-Chiari syndrome, RHF, Osler disease
  • Storage diseases: hemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency
  • Medications: methotrexate, amiodarone
  • Porphyria; fatty liver disease (alcoholic, NAFLD); veno-occlusive disease; neonatal hepatitis syndromes; cryptogenic (NASH)
Autoimmune hepatitis
  • Immune system attacks liver cells; asymptomatic, fatigue, nausea, pruritus
  • Ix: high IgG, anti-nuclear Ab, anti-smooth muscle Ab; biopsy – portal and periportal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate
  • Tx: prednisone, azathioprine
Alcoholic hepatitis

Reversible inflammatory liver damage from sustained, long-term alcohol consumption.

  • Direct toxicity from ethanol, its metabolites and oxidative damage disrupts cell and mitochondrial membranes → lipid accumulation
  • Classic presentation: symptomatic, nausea, malaise, tachycardia, fever
  • Hepatic failure/portal hypertension: ascites, coagulopathy, significant hematemesis from ruptured esophageal varices, encephalopathy (asterixis, altered mental status), RUQ tenderness, hepatomegaly
  • Dx: bloodwork (AST ≫ ALT, ↑ INR); histology (steatosis, neutrophilic infiltrate, centrilobular ballooning necrosis of hepatocytes, Mallory bodies)
  • Tx: abstinence, IV folate and thiamine, IV glucose, vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma, prednisolone

blocks.html:
Alcohol cirrhosis

Final, irreversible form of alcoholic liver disease.

  • Tx: abstinence; nutritional support (frequent small feeds, micronutrient/vitamin replacement, high protein and kcal); liver transplantation; psychosocial support; smoking cessation; avoid hepatotoxins; vaccinate (HAV, HBV, pneumococcus, influenza)
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)

Extra fat in liver cells, independent of alcohol use.

  • Causes: metabolic syndrome (DM, hypertension, central obesity, dyslipidemia), rapid weight loss, infections, drugs/toxins
  • Histology: microvesicular/macrovesicular steatosis → cellular ballooning → necrosis
  • Tx: lifestyle (diet, exercise), review medications, minimize EtOH, optimize comorbidities (statins are safe; screen for PCOS, hypothyroidism, OSA)
  • NASH: advanced NAFLD – the fat causes inflammation and scarring

blocks.html:
Cirrhosis

Irreversible scarring after years of chronic insult.

  • Cell death → progressive fibrosis → regenerative nodules; liver shrunken, firm, nodular
  • Severely impaired function: jaundice, pruritus, hypoalbuminemia, hypoestrogenism, anemia, coagulopathy, splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, portal hypertension
  • Dx: biopsy (gold standard); AST/ALT may be elevated or normal (hepatocytes “burn out”); ultrasound
  • Tx: liver transplantation

  • Tx: alcohol abstinence, avoid ACEI/ARB/NSAIDs, Na+ < 2 g/day, diuretics (spironolactone, furosemide), midodrine, fluid restrict if Na+ < 125, serial paracenteses + albumin, TIPS, liver transplant

Hepatic encephalopathy

Severe loss of hepatic function shunts blood around the liver → toxic metabolites accumulate → brain toxicity; often shows as asterixis.

  • Precipitants: GI bleeding, infection, electrolyte disturbance, constipation, sedatives, renal failure, dehydration, hypoglycemia, portal/hepatic vein thrombosis, HCC, hypoxia, non-compliance
  • Tx: reverse precipitants, start empirical Tx; lactulose, rifaximin; do NOT restrict protein or follow ammonia

Jaundice
  • Yellowing of skin and sclera from bilirubin deposition; bilirubin > 51.3 μmol/L (normal 3.1–17.1)
  • Common causes of ↑ bilirubin (HOT liver): hemolysis, obstruction, tumour, liver disease

• Absence of the canalicular protein multidrug-resistant protein 2 (MRP-2)
• Functionally normal, enlarged, black (dark) liver; asymptomatic, chronic/recurrent jaundice
• Dx: ↑ serum direct bilirubin, normal CBC, normal liver enzymes, grossly black liver on biopsy

Rotor syndrome: autosomal recessive condition caused by impaired hepatic storage of conjugated bilirubin, which leaks out
• Phenotypically similar to Dubin-Johnson syndrome, but milder presentation; normal (regular) liver

Alagille syndrome: autosomal dominant condition caused by too few bile ducts to drain the bile, which leads to bile build-up in the liver
• JAG1 or NOTCH2 gene mutations
• Prominent forehead, triangular face, butterfly vertebrae, posterior embryotoxon, tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary stenosis

rows: The 2 most common causes of a patient presenting with dysphagia and a documented history of weight loss are esophageal cancer and achalasia. Other causes of dysphagia, such as peptic stricture, are much less likely to result in significant weight loss unless very severe.

An EGD with esophageal biopsies needs to be considered in a patient with intermittent solid-food dysphagia to rule out eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) even in the presence of normal endoscopic findings. Eosinophil counts > 15 per hpf in the mid or proximal esophagus is extremely suggestive of EoE and can be treated with PPI, swallowed topical steroids & esophageal dilation.

The tip for today pertains to GI history taking. For any GI and liver-related illness, always ask about NSAIDs. It is also important to always take a detailed social history including smoking, alcohol, marijuana, and other recreational drug use. Don’t forget to elucidate any family history of GI related malignancy, IBD, celiac or liver disease. Finally, asking about any previous endoscopic evaluations can help to determine the need for further endoscopic investigation.

Typical symptoms of GERD (i.e. heartburn & regurgitation) are the most likely to respond to treatment with Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs). Other symptoms potentially associated with GERD include: cough, shortness of breath, hoarseness of voice and dental enamel erosion. These so called “extra esophageal” symptoms of GERD are less likely to respond to PPIs, mainly because they are less likely to be actually caused by GERD. If in doubt whether the symptoms are related to GERD or not, a 24 hour pH study can be helpful.

Cyclical attacks of nausea and vomiting, known as Cannabis Hyperemesis Syndrome (CHS), have been reported with the long-term use of marijuana; It is generally associated with heavy users of THC (i.e. Daily use for months to years) and patients often report compulsive bathing in hot water as this may relieve their symptoms. The only effective treatment is Cannabis cessation.

Weight loss is not a typical symptom of IBS, so in a patient presenting with possible IBS and weight loss other causes need to be excluded. For treatment of IBS always remember dietary interventions (i.e. low FODMAPs diet), psychosocial interventions and tailor medical therapy based on predominant symptom complex.

Always consider whether a digital rectal exam is necessary when examining a patient with GI symptoms. This simple exam is often overlooked and can be quite useful and even lifesaving if pathology such as a rectal mass is found. This should always be performed in a patient presenting with rectal bleeding. Ensure patients are informed about what you are going to be doing, obtain consent and drape patient appropriately. Remember to always have a chaperone present. There are very few contraindications to rectal exam: febrile neutropenia, no anus, no finger!

If suspicious for celiac disease, one can screen by ordering TTG antibodies. Always remember to order an IgA level anytime you order TTG antibodies, because TTG can be falsely negative if IgA is low. If TTG antibodies are positive, one should always go on to confirm the diagnosis with endoscopy and duodenal biopsies. Iron-deficiency anemia is the most common extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease.

When working up iron deficiency anemia, don’t forget to treat the iron deficiency while investigations are pending!! Do not use serum iron to diagnose iron deficiency anemia… use ferritin or transferrin saturation instead as they are a more reliable indicator of actual iron stores.

Remember melena is more typical of an Upper GI bleed but occasionally can be a manifestation of a proximal Lower GI bleed. Similarly, bright red blood per rectum, is usually a manifestation of a lower GI bleed, but one always needs to be alert to the possibility that it represents a brisk Upper GI bleed, which would be suggested if the patient is hemodynamically unstable. The most important management principal for GI bleeds is to always resuscitate the patient aggressively first, then consider scoping them!

All patients with chronic liver disease, with or without cirrhosis, should be vaccinated for Hep A and Hep B, unless they have active infection or are serologically immune. If a patient with compensated liver disease were to acquire an active infection with either Hepatitis A or Hepatitis B, this can lead to severe decompensation and this can be prevented through vaccination.

Early liver cirrhosis can be present with a normal appearing liver on imaging in addition to normal liver enzymes and synthetic liver bloodwork. High clinical suspicion is necessary. Unexplained splenomegaly, dilated portal vein, and thrombocytopenia can be early clues to the presence of cirrhosis.

Statins are safe to use in patients with cirrhosis. Liver enzymes should be routinely monitored, and these medications can be continued as long as liver enzymes do not elevate more than 2 times from baseline after starting statins.

Patients with acute pancreatitis needs fluids – lots of it. Ringer’s lactate is generally preferred, and patients often require 4-5L of fluid to make up for their fluid deficit. They also require pain control and reintroduction of nutrition as soon as they are able to tolerate it (i.e. symptoms improving). Typically they should be progressed from clear fluids to full fluids to diet as tolerated. If symptoms recur with reintroduction of food, then you may have to back off temporarily and if prolonged NPO is expected or required may need to consider supplemental nutrition with NJ tube or rarely TPN.

In patients with hepatic encephalopathy ammonia does not correlate with the degree of encephalopathy and should not be used in the diagnosis, rather the clinical assessment is key in making the diagnosis.

Pancreatic pseudocyst

Collection of pancreatic juice walled by fibrous or granulation tissue, in or around the pancreas after pancreatitis or ductal leak; takes > 4 weeks to form; no epithelial lining.

  • Abdominal pain, vomiting, jaundice, recurrent pancreatitis
  • Complications: infection, hemorrhage, rupture
  • Tx: conservative if asymptomatic; drain if symptoms/complications (endoscopic, percutaneous, surgical)
Cystic pancreatic lesions
  • Ductal adenocarcinomas, neuroendocrine tumours and solid pseudopapillary neoplasms may become cystic
  • Serous cystic neoplasm: F > M, body or tail, almost always benign; DDx = metastatic renal cell carcinoma
  • Mucinous cystic neoplasm: F, body or tail, larger cysts, mucinous cells over ovarian-type stroma; may become malignant
  • Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm: M > F, head of pancreas, ducts dilated by papillae lined by mucinous cells; may become malignant

Other upper GI pathologies
  • Mallory-Weiss syndrome: longitudinal lacerations at the GE junction from severe vomiting (alcohol use disorder, bulimia nervosa); painful hematemesis
  • Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: multiple peptic ulcers in stomach and duodenum from excess gastrin secreted by a gastrinoma → excess acid; associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 1
Gastroparesis

Objectively delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction.

  • Nausea, vomiting, early satiety, bloating, upper abdominal pain, weight loss
  • Etiology: type 1 diabetes (longstanding, poor control), idiopathic (1/3), post-viral (norovirus, rotavirus), medications (opioids, TCAs, CCBs, dopamine agonists, anticholinergics), post-surgical, neurologic (MS, Parkinson’s), autoimmune (scleroderma), hypothyroidism
  • Ix: EGD, CT enterography/small bowel follow-through; gastric emptying study – normal 2 hr < 60% retained; 4 hr < 10% (mild 10–15%, moderate 15–35%, severe > 35%)
  • Tx: low-fat, low-fibre diet; small frequent meals 4–5×/day; avoid carbonated drinks, alcohol, smoking; tight glycemic control; antiemetics (5-HT3 antagonists); promotility drugs (domperidone, metoclopramide, erythromycin) – lowest dose, drug holidays (2 wks q 3 months), cycle rather than combine, monitor DDIs/QT
Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome
  • Chronic heavy cannabis use (~1 g/day) → repeated severe vomiting
  • Temporary relief from hot baths or showers; resolves after stopping cannabis
  • Tx: stop cannabis (6 months), haloperidol, topical capsaicin cream
Lactose intolerance
  • Lactase (brush border enzyme) deficiency: primary (↓ expression), secondary (after enteric infection, 4–6 weeks), congenital
  • Osmotic diarrhea (unabsorbed lactose), bloating, flatus (bacterial fermentation)
  • Tx: avoid milk products, lactase supplements
Functional dyspepsia (indigestion)

≥ 12 weeks of ≥ 1 of bothersome postprandial fullness, early satiety, epigastric pain or epigastric burning, with no structural disease (normal gastroscopy).

  • DDx: GERD, PUD, drug-induced (ASA/NSAIDs), H. pylori gastritis, gastric cancer, biliary tract disease, pancreatic disease
  • Red flags: onset > 40, GI bleeding, abdominal mass, vomiting, weight loss, nocturnal pain, dysphagia
  • Ix: CBC, stool occult blood, H. pylori serology, ultrasound; endoscopy if red flags or failed empiric therapy
  • Tx: reassurance/education, diet, lifestyle (exercise, ↓ caffeine/alcohol, smoking cessation, weight loss), stress management; acid suppression (PPIs, H2 antagonists); tricyclic antidepressants; treat the underlying cause

blocks.html:
Abdominal pain workup
  • Hx: timing, severity, location, acuity, exacerbating factors, associated symptoms, PMHx, gynecological Hx, sexual Hx, medications, substance use, travel Hx
  • PEx: vitals, inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation, pelvic exam, DRE, CVS and respiratory exam
  • Ix: bloodwork (CBC, electrolytes, liver enzymes, LFTs, lipase, β-HCG, CRP, lactate, urinalysis); imaging (AXR/CXR, ultrasound, CT abdomen/pelvis); ECG, troponins
Acute (surgical) abdomen

Abdominal pain and physical findings indicate the patient needs surgical management.

Peritonitis

Inflammation of the peritoneum; gradual or abrupt onset of severe, constant pain.

  • PEx: percussion tenderness, shake tenderness, rebound tenderness, involuntary guarding, rigidity
  • Generalized (> 1 quadrant) – surgical; focal (single quadrant) – may be managed non-surgically
  • Ix: Hb, WBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lipase, bilirubin, liver enzymes, β-HCG; AXR, CT, ultrasound
  • Tx: IV fluids, NPO, broad-spectrum ABX, prepare for the OR
Causes of an acute abdomen

1. Perforation – free air outside the bowel lumen (under the diaphragm on upright CXR)

  • Hx: NSAIDs, PUD (duodenal > gastric), dyspepsia, previous endoscopies, diverticular disease, chronic constipation, recent weight loss, ↓ appetite, FHx of cancer
  • Tx: Graham patch (duodenum), resection + primary anastomosis, Hartmann’s procedure (severe diverticular disease)

2. Ischemic bowel (splanchnic vascular occlusive disease) – SMA most common

  • Embolic (atrial fibrillation, previous MI) > thrombotic (atherosclerotic risk)
  • Sudden severe mid-abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, explosive diarrhea
  • PEx: pain out of proportion to exam, fever, tachycardia, unwell-appearing
  • Ix: ↑ lactate, ↑ inflammatory markers, acute renal failure
  • Tx: fluid resuscitation, NPO, ABX, surgical resection

3. Bowel obstruction – anatomical disturbance preventing passage of gas and stool for 12–24 hrs

  • Obstipation: failure to pass stool and gas
  • Always evaluate: prior surgical scars (adhesions), hernias, masses (neoplasm), DRE
  • Ischemia or impending perforation (FATAL): fever, acidosis (↑ lactate), tachycardia, abdominal pain, leukocytosis

lectures.title: Acute Abdomen, Obstruction & Esophageal Disease
lectures.framing: The approach to abdominal pain is to decide first whether this is an acute (surgical) abdomen – perforation, ischemia, obstruction or bleeding – then work up the rest. The lecture also covers congenital gut anomalies and the major esophageal diseases.
lectures.keypoints: Generalized peritonitis = OR; focal may be managed medically. Mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion, ↑ lactate, SMA embolus most often; small-bowel ischemia mortality 55–85%. Obstruction red flags: FATAL. Adhesive SBO: 85% non-operative; non-adhesive SBO and LBO go to surgery. Duodenal atresia = double bubble, Down syndrome. Achalasia = bird-beak; GERD → Barrett → adenocarcinoma.

blocks.html:
• Appendix = congenital true diverticulum (all 4 layers); colonic diverticula = acquired false
  • Appendicitis: midgut/SMA → umbilical → RLQ pain; young, recent URTI. Diverticulitis: hindgut/IMA → suprapubic → LLQ; rare < 35
  • Appendicitis → surgery usually; diverticulitis → usually not
  • Diverticulitis: uncomplicated = outpatient (ABX, or NSAIDs alone, no colonoscopy); abscess < 5 cm = admit + IV ABX; > 5 cm = percutaneous drain; perforation/shock = urgent OR
  • Diverticular bleeding is painless – never during a diverticulitis attack
